summary: Written after an IETF BOF on how the Next Generation of IP should be chosen. It discusses the lack of clear direction and the issues to resolve toward an IPng decision. It was submitted in response to RFC 1550 and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: People argued about how to pick the internet's next address system. This note says what needs deciding.

subtitle: How to organize the effort to pick the next version of IP

tldr.problem: The IETF was struggling to decide how to choose the next generation of IP, with disagreement about process, timeline, and scope.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes a new temporary IESG area dedicated to IPng, with Area Directors overseeing technical work on timing constraints, scope, criteria, and candidate proposals.
tldr.outcome: This organizational structure set the framework for the eventual selection of IPv6 as the next generation IP protocol.

today: RFC 1719 is Informational and describes the process that led to the adoption of IPv6 as the next generation IP. The IESG area and directorate structure it established successfully guided the IPng selection and remains a model for major protocol decisions in the IETF.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: After a 1994 IETF meeting in Amsterdam, the community held a special meeting called the IPDecide BOF to discuss choosing the next generation of IP. The meeting showed that while the community recognized the need for a new IP protocol, there was no clear consensus on how to make the decision or what criteria to use. The community was uncertain about the urgency of the problem and whether the IETF or the marketplace should make the final choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers knew they needed a new internet address system, but did not agree on how to pick it.

sections.title: A Direction for IPng
sections.content:
The RFC announces key decisions about the IPng process. The IETF will move toward closure by taking active steps toward a technical decision, rather than waiting for market forces. The IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) will take responsibility for developing an IPng recommendation. The process will be open and published well in advance. The community will have ample opportunity to review and comment on the recommendation before it is finalized.

A new temporary IESG area is created specifically for IPng, with two co-Area Directors: Allison Mankin from NRL and Scott Bradner from Harvard. An IPng Directorate will act as a direction-setting body to bring additional viewpoints into the process. All existing IPng-related working groups are moved into this new area.
sections.plainLanguage: The leaders decided to set up a team that will gather information and make a recommendation to the community.

sections.title: Key Issues to Resolve
sections.content:
Two critical issues must be addressed before making an IPng recommendation. First, the scope question: should IPng address only known scaling and address exhaustion problems, or should it also include advanced features like resource reservation for real-time traffic? Advocates for including advanced features argue that migrating to a new IP happens only rarely and all advanced features should be considered. Opponents argue that time pressure from address exhaustion may not allow full exploration of advanced features.

Second, the timeframe question: how urgent is the need for IPng? The answer depends on the current rate of address assignments, address assignment policies, the impact of CIDR aggregation, the time needed to develop IPng, and the time required to deploy and migrate to the new protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The team needed to decide two things: what should the new system do, and how much time do we have to build it.

sections.title: Work Plan
sections.content:
The RFC outlines specific activities for the new Area Directors and Directorate. They must develop an understanding of the available timeframe by reviewing Internet growth metrics, analyzing the impact of CIDR address aggregation, developing guidelines for classless Internet addressing, and estimating the time required for development, deployment and migration. Based on this timeframe analysis, they will make a recommendation on IPng scope: whether to focus on scaling issues alone or include advanced features.

The team will also develop a clear set of technical requirements and decision criteria for IPng (building on the IESG statement in RFC 1380) and make a recommendation on which current IPng candidates to accept, if any. Regular progress reports are required, with a detailed report at the next IETF plenary.
sections.plainLanguage: They will collect data about when we will run out of addresses, decide what features to include, write down the rules for judging proposals, and then pick the winner.

references.text: Carpenter, B., "IPDecide BOF Minutes", IETF directories, July 1993.
